title: Content pages: newsletter, podcast, community, evidence, contact, history
summary: These six pages have no captures yet, so this surface holds references and judging criteria only. Today /newsletter, /podcast and /community are a name, one paragraph of 17 or 18 words and one button each; they name the vendor but not what arrives, how often, or what an issue or episode is like. /contact names four routes in plain words but gives no reply time, /evidence-based-care opens with a definition and reads like a policy, and the founder's letter on /history runs to 619 words under headings that are partly labels. The references show how shipped sites say these things in few words: a promise with its rhythm, an episode with its length, a reply time, a letter that starts with the reader.

references.pattern: Newsletter hero: a six-word promise, one line with the name and how often, one email field
references.why: The headline is the feeling, 'A deep breath for your inbox' (6 words). One line under it carries everything else in 16: 'Subscribe to our monthly newsletter, Breathing Space, for updates, resources, and insight for workplace wellness enthusiasts.' The reader knows its name, how often it comes and what is in it before she reaches the form. The form asks for one thing, the email, and the button says 'Subscribe'.
references.apply: The /newsletter hero in the same three parts: a headline of eight words or fewer about what the reader gets, one line of 20 words or fewer with the name Femme Focus, how often it arrives and what is in it, then one email field and 'Subscribe'. Today's body says 'Subscribe on Beehiiv—no Eleva account required' and never says how often. Leave out Calm's 'here' as link text; write 'Read our privacy policy'. This is Calm's page for employers, hence 'Work Email'; Eleva asks for 'Email'.
references.query: newsletter landing page hero section for a wellness app

references.pattern: A named letter: what it is and how often in 15 words, then each issue as number, date, title, teaser and 'Read the issue'
references.why: Under the name 'Population Report', one sentence says what arrives and when: 'A weekly letter about trading cards, collectibles, and the slow-motion collision between culture and capital.' (15 words). Each issue below is a row: 'Issue 001', the date, a title of six words ('Not all cardboard is created equal.'), a teaser of 22 words in the letter's own voice, and a link that names the action, 'Read the issue'. The reader can judge the writing before she gives an email.
references.apply: Call Femme Focus a letter and describe it in one sentence: who writes it, what about, how often. Under the sign-up, list the last three issues with date, title, a teaser of 25 words or fewer taken from the issue itself, and 'Read the issue'. Trading card company; kept for structure. The grey type on grey is hard to read and is not for Eleva.
references.query: newsletter page with a list of past issues

references.pattern: 'Previous editions': each past issue shown as its own opening lines, with its date and one link
references.why: The heading is two words, 'Previous editions'. Each of four cards shows the top of the real email, so the subject line is the title ('Soundscapes, graphic generators, and Spotify Wrapped design'), with the date under it ('Dec 7, 2022') and one link, 'Open browser version'. Nothing is described; the issue speaks for itself. 'Next' pages back through older ones.
references.apply: A 'Past issues' row on /newsletter: three or four cards, each the issue's own title and first lines, its date, and one link, 'Read this issue'. It answers 'what will I get?' with the thing itself and needs no extra copy. Web design tool; kept for the pattern.
references.query: newsletter page with a list of past issues

references.pattern: Podcast page: one episode ready to play, 'Listen on' as one line, and the episode list beside it
references.why: The player card holds a label ('Teaser'), the title 'Introducing Heart of Business', two sentences that open with the show's question ('Who are the greatest teams in business and how are they connecting with their customers in inspiring ways?') and a play bar. Directly under it sits one line: 'Listen on: Apple Podcasts, Spotify, & Google Podcasts'. The 'Episode List' beside it gives each episode a number, a title and two links, 'Listen' and 'Open'.
references.apply: On /podcast, put one episode to play first, with a two-sentence summary that starts with the question the episode answers. Then one line, 'Listen on: Spotify, Apple Podcasts, YouTube', as text links, in place of today's 'Listen on your favourite platform'. List episodes by number and title. Customer email software; kept for structure.
references.query: podcast landing page with episode list

references.pattern: Episode card: guest, title, 'Episode 21 | date | 27 min', three lines of summary and four one-word actions
references.why: The section opens with one 16-word line on who speaks and why: 'Product design leaders and experts share the experiences and learnings that shaped their path to success.' Each card then answers what a listener asks: who (photo and name), what (the title), how long ('EPISODE 21 | 07 DECEMBER 2022 | 27 MIN'), and a summary cut at three lines with 'See more'. The actions are single words that name what happens: 'Listen', 'Subscribe', 'Transcript', 'Share'.
references.apply: Each Eleva episode as a card: the guest's photo, name and profession, the title, 'Episode 4 · 12 March · 27 min', a summary of 40 words or fewer and 'Listen'. Offer 'Transcript' when there is one, so the episode can be read as well as heard. Product research tool; kept for the card.
references.query: podcast landing page with episode list

references.pattern: Community hero that says who it is for, what you do there, and where it lives
references.why: The headline names the group in four words, 'The Journey Management Community'. One sentence of 23 words lists what people do there: 'share your knowledge, ask questions, and learn how teams are using TheyDo'. The button is 'Join the community', and the next heading says where, 'Join us on Slack', so nobody is surprised by the place they land.
references.apply: On /community, say in one sentence who is there and what you do there ('Talk with other members about each issue and episode'), and say once, beside the button, where it opens. Today's copy says 'The community lives on Beehiiv today; Eleva accounts are optional', which explains the set-up and not the benefit. Button: 'Join the community', not 'Open community'. Journey mapping software; kept for structure. 'Pioneers' is a word Eleva leaves out.

references.pattern: Community rules introduced as a welcome, in two sentences
references.why: The rules block does not open with rules. It opens with reassurance in 20 words: 'If you have a question, no matter how basic or how technical, you're in the right place to get help.' Then 14 more on why guidelines exist: 'Here are a few guidelines to make sure everyone can enjoy their time here.' The block above it is the caution: its heading, 'Welcome to the Dropbox Community', is repeated as the first five words of its own paragraph, and both links say 'Read more'.
references.apply: Before a member joins a health community she wants to know it is safe to ask. Give /community a short block: one sentence that no question is too small, one on what the guidelines protect, and a link named 'Read the community guidelines'. Do not repeat the heading in the first line under it. File storage product; kept for the copy.

references.pattern: Science page hero: a three-word title and a 36-word lead on why the company studies its own work
references.why: 'Science at Headspace' is three words and tells the reader where she is. The lead does not claim to be proven; it gives the reason for research in plain words: 'the only way to know if we're truly accomplishing that is to measure, test, and study it. That's where our research comes in.' It is first person, has no citation and no jargon, and the hero has no button to compete with it.
references.apply: Open /evidence-based-care as a person would say it: a short title ('How we work from evidence') and a lead of 40 words or fewer in the first person, on why Eleva's experts work from research and what that means for your session. Today the page starts with a definition ('Evidence-based care means that experts ground recommendations in published research, clinical guidelines, and their professional judgement') and its summary line reads 'Platform role, expert judgement, and selected references'. Meditation app; a health neighbour.
references.query: science and research page hero section for a health app

references.pattern: 'About our editorial process': who writes, who checks, and one promise, in two short paragraphs
references.why: The heading names the reader's question in four words. The first paragraph answers in short sentences and ends on the promise that matters: 'every word is checked by an expert before it's published' (10 words). The second says who the authors and reviewers are, by profession, and closes with what the reader can count on: 'relevant, accurate, and high quality'. About 90 words in all.
references.apply: A short block on /evidence-based-care, linked from /newsletter and /podcast: who writes, who reviews (by profession), and one line such as 'A licensed expert reviews every piece before we publish it', if that is true today. Take the positive sentences only; Dovetail's 'No complicated jargon' and 'No content written by AI-powered robots' say what it is not, and Eleva says what it does. Research software; kept for the copy.

references.pattern: Research as a short list: title, what kind of file, and a button that says what will happen
references.why: Under 'Research in action' and one line of lead, each source is a row: a picture, the title, a small line with the format ('PDF • 20mb' or 'Web Page') and one button. The button changes with the row: 'Download' for a file, 'Go to link' for a page. The reader knows what she will get before she presses.
references.apply: Turn the numbered references at the foot of /evidence-based-care into rows: the source's name, one line on what it is and why Eleva's advisors use it, and a link that says where it goes ('Read on who.int', 'Download the guideline, PDF'). Today they read 'WHO digital health guidelines — who.int'. Telehealth brand in the United States; kept for the list. Its lead ('Dive into the latest research and in-depth analysis') is the kind of line Eleva leaves out.
references.query: research reports list section with download buttons for a health company

references.pattern: Contact page as routes: a short title, one line, one named action, and a line for 'none of these'
references.why: Under 'Contact us', one 12-word sentence gives the quickest way: 'The fastest way to reach us is to send us a message.' Each main route is a card with a title of two or three words, one line of ten words or fewer ('Get support': 'Report an issue or get help.') and a button that repeats the route ('Contact support', 'Contact sales'). The page ends with a way out for everyone else: 'If your inquiry does not match one of the above departments, contact support using this form or send a question to hello@tines.com.'
references.apply: Eleva's four routes already have plain titles ('Bookings and your account', 'Privacy and your data'). Give each a link that names the action ('Write to support', 'Write about your data'), put the route most members need first and larger, and close with one line: 'Not sure who to write to? Write to support and we will pass it on.' Workflow software for security teams; kept for structure. 'Departments' and 'inquiry' are office words Eleva leaves out.
references.query: Figma contact us page with talk to sales team and get support

references.pattern: Contact hero in two words, with the reply time in the next line
references.why: 'Say hello.' is two words. The line beside it is 13 and holds the promise: 'A question, an idea, a concrete project. I reply within two working days.' The form explains itself as it goes: under Phone, 'Optional, if you would rather talk.'; under the message, 'I only use your details to answer your enquiry. More in the privacy policy.' The button says 'Send message'.
references.apply: Eleva's contact lead says 'We read every message and reply in English, Portuguese or Spanish' but not when. Add the reply time in plain words ('We reply within two working days') once the team confirms it. If a form is added: give optional fields a reason, say in one line how the details are used, and label the button 'Send message'. One-person design studio; kept for the copy. Eleva writes 'we'.
references.query: contact page section with a message form and reply time

references.pattern: A contact introduction that lowers the pressure, with opening hours beside it
references.why: A therapy provider opens its contact page with 25 words in a human voice: 'Whether you're looking for support, curious about our programs, or just have a question, we're always happy to talk. No pressure. Just people who care.' Email, phone and 'Business Hours Monday–Friday, 9am–5pm PST' sit under it, so the reader knows when someone will answer. The form is the caution: a 'terms and conditions' tick box on a contact form, and a button that says 'Submit'.
references.apply: Someone writing to a health company may be worried. Eleva's contact page can say, in one or two sentences, that any question is welcome and that a person reads it, and give the hours the team answers. Keep it to 25 words. Leave out the terms tick box, and name the button for what it does. Therapy services for families; the closest in subject to Eleva.
references.query: contact page section with a message form and reply time

references.pattern: Founders' letter that begins with the reader's day, titled with its belief and signed by first names
references.why: The title is the belief, in seven words: 'Health isn't something that happens to you'. The letter opens 'Hey there,' and its first sentence is about the reader, not the company: 'If you're reading this, you're probably like us—spending most of your days juggling work, family, and trying to stay healthy.' Paragraphs are one to three sentences. It ends with an invitation ('give Bevel a try and let us know what you think!'), three first names, 'Co-Founders of Bevel', and one photo of them together.
references.apply: Eleva's letter on /history is 619 words under six headings and opens with the founder ('Hi! I'm Patrícia Mota'). Keep her voice, and let the first lines meet the reader where she is: the question nobody answered, the advice that did not fit. Title the page with the belief, not 'The story behind Eleva Care'. Close with one invitation and both first names. Bevel's letter is about 500 words and spends five paragraphs on the history of medicine; Eleva's can be shorter. Health tracking app; a health neighbour.
references.query: Bevel health app letter from the co-founders

references.pattern: A founder's story in eight short chapters, each headed in her own words
references.why: The story is cut into chapters of one or two short paragraphs, and the headings read as a story on their own: 'Why do we care so much?', 'Finance has always made me feel insecure', 'Is this the best we can do?', 'Getting off the ground', 'Runway today'. Two are questions and one is a confession. The first line is a person speaking: 'Hi! I'm Siqi, one of the founders of Runway. I was 23 when I started running my first company'. A reader who only scans the headings still gets the whole arc.
references.apply: Eleva's headings on /history are partly labels ('The academic journey', 'Our mission'). Rewrite them as the founder's own sentences, so they tell the story when read alone: 'I didn't have answers when the women I treated became pregnant', 'The evidence existed. It wasn't reaching women.', 'So we built Eleva'. Keep each chapter to two paragraphs; 'The team I'm proud of' has five today. Financial planning software; kept for structure.
references.query: Runway company story section told in chapters by the founder

references.pattern: An empty page that says what will appear and gives one next step
references.why: With nothing to list, the page still has a headline of four words, 'Build the perfect trip', and 14 words that explain the space: 'Explore homes, experiences, and services. When you book, your reservations will show up here.' One button follows, and one quiet link for the other case, 'Find past trips in your profile'. It never says 'nothing here' or 'coming soon'.
references.apply: Where a content page has nothing to show yet (no episode embedded on /podcast, no past issues on /newsletter), say what will appear and offer the one thing the reader can do now: 'New episodes appear here. Get a note when the next one is out.' with 'Subscribe to Femme Focus'. Airbnb's button says 'Get started'; Eleva's names the action. Signed-in screen from a travel marketplace; kept for the copy.
references.query: Airbnb trips page with no trips booked

references.pattern: Community hero where a small label carries the name and the headline speaks to the reader
references.why: The name sits in a small label, 'ZENDESK COMMUNITY', which frees the headline to reassure in five words: 'You're in the right place'. The button is two words, 'Join us'. The paragraph is the caution: 34 words that say 'connect', 'engage', 'come together', 'learn from your peers' and 'grow your network' for one idea.
references.apply: On /community and /newsletter the heading today is only the name ('Femme Focus community', 'Femme Focus by Eleva'), and the small label above it only repeats the page ('Community', 'Newsletter'). Put the name in the label and use the heading for the reader: 'You're among women asking the same questions'. Then one sentence, not five verbs. Zendesk writes 'users'; Eleva writes 'members'. Customer service software; kept for the pattern.

judging_criteria: Is the hero a heading of eight words or fewer and one lead of 25 words or fewer, with nothing else before the first action? (14-content-pages/01 Calm, 14-content-pages/12 Metic)

Does each section hold one idea under a heading that says it, in two short paragraphs or fewer, and on /history do the headings tell the story when read alone? (14-content-pages/15 Runway, 14-content-pages/09 Dovetail)

Does every button and link name what happens next ('Subscribe', 'Listen', 'Read the issue', 'Send message'), with no 'Read more', 'Learn more', 'Submit', 'Get started' or 'here'? (14-content-pages/02 Tash, 14-content-pages/05 Maze, 14-content-pages/12 Metic)
Is each fact said once on the page: no heading repeated in the first line under it, and no promise made in the hero and again in the body? (14-content-pages/07 Dropbox, 14-content-pages/17 Zendesk)

Is the page free of internal and legal words (platform integrity, clinical artefacts, exercising your rights under the GDPR), is a vendor named only where the reader will land on its site, and are readers called members? (14-content-pages/09 Dovetail, 14-content-pages/06 TheyDo)
Does the newsletter sign-up ask only for an email, and say beside the field what arrives and how often? (14-content-pages/01 Calm, 14-content-pages/02 Tash)

Does the newsletter, podcast or community page show at least one real issue, episode or topic with its date or length, or, when there is none yet, say what will appear there and offer one action? (14-content-pages/03 Webflow, 14-content-pages/04 Front, 14-content-pages/05 Maze, 14-content-pages/16 Airbnb)

Does /contact give a reply time in plain words, and one clear route for a reader who is not sure who to write to? (14-content-pages/12 Metic, 14-content-pages/11 Tines, 14-content-pages/13 Maxima Therapy)
